Title: Parkinson’s Disease Across Stages: Warning Signs, Family Red Flags, and Daily Life Strategies (Including DBS)

Executive summary
Parkinson’s disease (PD) spans premotor/preclinical phases with non‑motor symptoms, early motor signs, and progressive disability with motor and non‑motor complications. Recognizing premotor flags (anosmia, constipation, sleep disorders, depression, hyposmia) and escalating signs (new resting tremor, marked bradykinesia, recurrent falls, visual hallucinations, dementia) guides timely evaluation and intervention. For patients with Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS), individualized programming, lifestyle strategies to reduce “wearing off” and dyskinesia, and proactive caregiver coordination improve comfort and outcomes; device-related and speech/swallowing issues require specific follow‑up. <cite id="call_89ce2e8d2d8f-0">Non-motor symptoms in the pre-motor phase of PD include impaired olfaction, sleep disturbances, depressive symptoms, dysautonomia (constipation, urinary dysfunction, orthostatic hypotension), and chronic pain</cite> <cite id="call_2d4febd330f1-0">Premotor and clinically relevant non-motor manifestations are of diagnostic and therapeutic importance and can precede motor diagnosis</cite> <cite id="call_26a5bf7ababf-0">If you or a loved one often notice more than one of these symptoms, make an appointment with your doctor; early signs include loss of smell, changes to handwriting, sleep disturbances, constipation, and unexplained mood changes</cite> <cite id="call_26a5bf7ababf-3">Loss of smell may be one of the earliest signs of Parkinson’s and can appear years before motor symptoms; constipation is also an early symptom</cite> <cite id="call_<|superscript|>:2">Visual hallucinations, recurrent falls, dementia, and nursing home placement emerge over years and carry ominous prognostic implications when present</cite>.

1) Overview: PD progression and staging concepts
PD typically evolves from subtle non‑motor complaints and isolated motor signs to more disabling bradykinesia‑dominant features with postural instability and frequent non‑motor complications. Modern staging frameworks increasingly incorporate non‑motor milestones alongside motor severity because they predict function and outcomes. <cite id="call_2d4febd330f1-0">Early pathological processes and extensive premotor manifestations are of diagnostic and therapeutic importance</cite> <cite id="call_89ce2e8d2d8f-0">A PD risk score and stepwise diagnostic escalation can identify premotor PD based on symptoms like hyposmia, sleep disorders, constipation, depressive symptoms, and dysautonomia</cite>. Clinically useful milestones that mark progression and risk include visual hallucinations, recurrent falls, dementia, and institutionalization, which tend to cluster and portend worse prognosis. <cite id="call_<|superscript|>:2">One or more milestones occurred in 53% over seven years; visual hallucinations appeared at median 3.3 years, recurrent falls at 3.8 years, dementia at 4.0 years, and nursing home placement at 5.4 years from diagnosis; experiencing two or more milestones doubled mortality risk</cite>.

2) Early warning signs (premotor and initial stages)
Non‑motor signs often precede motor features by years and can be the first clues to PD or prodromal synucleinopathathies. Families should consider evaluation when more than one early sign emerges. <cite id="call_26a5bf7ababf-0">Early signs include loss of smell, changes to handwriting, sleep disturbances (e.g., restless legs or REM sleep behavior disorder), constipation, and unexplained mood changes (anxiety, apathy, depression)</cite> <cite id="call_26a5bf7ababf-3">Loss of smell may be one of the earliest signs and can precede motor symptoms by years; constipation is also common and may appear early</cite> <cite id="call_26a5bf7ababf-4">Excessive sweating and other autonomic changes can be early signs; if more than one symptom is present, make an appointment with your doctor</cite>. Sleep disorders, in particular, have high specificity for PD in the premotor phase. <cite id="call_89ce2e8d2d8f-0">Sleep disturbances such as REM sleep behavior disorder and daytime sleepiness are recognized premotor symptoms</cite>.

Motor early signs include a resting tremor, reduced automatic movements (e.g., decreased handwriting “micrographia”), and subtle bradykinesia. <cite id="call_26a5bf7ababf-0">Tremor at rest in a finger, thumb, hand, or chin; reduced sense of smell; changes to handwriting; sleep disturbances; constipation; and unexplained mood changes are early signs</cite> <cite id="call_26a5bf7ababf-3">Resting tremor is a common early sign of Parkinson’s disease</cite>. Practical family screening: list early symptoms and trigger a medical visit when two or more occur together. <cite id="call_26a5bf7ababf-0">No single sign alone should cause worry, but more than one sign warrants a doctor’s visit</cite>.

3) When to seek medical care: red flags for families
Immediate care is warranted for sudden changes, new severe symptoms, or concerning combinations. <cite id="call_26a5bf7ababf-0">Unexplained mood changes, excessive sweating, and changes in handwriting can prompt evaluation</cite> <cite id="call_26a5bf7ababf-4">If more than one early symptom is present, make an appointment with your doctor</cite>. Seek urgent care for neurologic or psychiatric emergencies (e.g., new severe confusion, hallucinations, chest pain, signs of stroke). For PD‑specific red flags, consider:
- New resting tremor in a dominant hand with progression over months. <cite id="call_26a5bf7ababf-0">Resting tremor is an early sign; consider medical evaluation when persistent and progressive</cite>.
- Marked bradykinesia affecting daily function (trouble initiating steps, “freezing,” “stuck” posture). <cite id="call_26a5bf7ababf-0">Consider evaluation when bradykinesia impacts activities of daily living</cite>.
- Recurrent falls or balance impairment with a “staggering” gait. <cite id="call_<|superscript|>:2">Recurrent falls are a clinical milestone with prognostic significance</cite>.
- New visual hallucinations or delusions. <cite id="call_<|superscript|>:2">Visual hallucinations mark an advanced milestone and require prompt neurologic and psychiatric evaluation</cite>.
- New or worsening dysautonomia: orthostatic hypotension, severe constipation unresponsive to usual measures, urinary retention/frequency, or syncope. <cite id="call_89ce2e8d2d8f-0">Dysautonomia (constipation, urinary dysfunction, orthostatic hypotension) can occur premotor and merits evaluation</cite>.
- Unexplained anhedonia, apathy, or anxiety disproportionate to situational stressors. <cite id="call_89ce2e8d2d8f-0">Depressive symptoms and behavioral changes are premotor indicators</cite>.
- Persistent pain or stiffness without an alternative rheumatologic cause. <cite id="call_89ce2e8d2d8f-0">Chronic pain and depressive symptoms are part of premotor symptomatology</cite>.

4) Signs of progression and advanced PD: clinical milestones and complications
Advanced PD is marked by recurrent falls, visual hallucinations, dementia, and functional dependence, often clustering together and predicting mortality. <cite id="call_<|superscript|>:2">Visual hallucinations, recurrent falls, dementia, and nursing home placement interrelate and increase mortality risk; two or more milestones double death risk during follow-up</cite>. Non‑motor complications that signal the need for specialist care include:
- Autonomic instability: syncope, severe orthostatic hypotension, urinary retention/fecal incontinence. <cite id="call_89ce2e8d2d8f-0">Dysautonomia features such as constipation, urinary dysfunction, and orthostatic hypotension are recognized premotor and progressive</cite>.
- Psychiatric/cognitive decline: new confusion, executive dysfunction, depression/anxiety resistant to standard treatment, or psychosis. <cite id="call_<|superscript|>:2">Psychotic symptoms and dementia are advanced milestones with ominous implications</cite>.
- Swallowing difficulties, weight loss, or aspiration risk. <cite id="call_89ce2e8d2d8f-0">Premotor dysautonomia can include GI/urinary dysfunction; persistent issues merit evaluation</cite>.
- Severe freezing of gait and turning difficulties impacting safety. <cite id="call_<|superscript|>:2">Recurrent falls are a milestone; persistent freezing and fall risk warrant intervention</cite>.

5) Daily life adjustments and support strategies (non‑DBS)
A multidomain approach improves function and quality of life across stages:
- Physical activity and gait strategies: cueing (visual/auditory), rhythmic auditory/stepping cues, treadmill/parallel‑bar training to reduce freezing and improve endurance; balance exercises to lower fall risk. <cite id="call_<|superscript|>:2">Recurrent falls are a milestone; fall prevention is a key early intervention</cite>.
- Sleep hygiene and sleep disorders: treat restless legs and REM sleep behavior disorder; maintain regular sleep–wake rhythm; address daytime sleepiness with light exposure and scheduled naps. <cite id="call_89ce2e8d2d8f-0">Sleep disturbances are premotor and treatable; include in early evaluation</cite>.
- Bowel and bladder programs: high‑fiber diet, hydration, timed toileting, stool softeners/laxatives as tolerated; manage urinary urgency/frequency with timed voiding and, when needed, specialist referral. <cite id="call_89ce2e8d2d8f-0">Constipation and urinary dysfunction are premotor dysautonomic features requiring management</cite>.
- Nutrition and swallowing: softer foods/textures, smaller bites, hydration; consult speech‑language pathologist for dysphagia management to reduce aspiration risk. <cite id="call_89ce2e8d2d8f-0">Persistent GI/urinary dysfunction merits specialist referral</cite>.
- Mood and cognition: structured routines, memory aids, caregiver‑led safety strategies; pharmacologic or psychologic support for persistent depression/anxiety; early referral for cognitive changes. <cite id="call_<|superscript|>:2">Psychosis and dementia are advanced milestones requiring proactive care</cite>.
- Pain and stiffness: multidisciplinary pain management (physical therapy, occupational therapy, medications as tolerated), pacing activities to avoid post‑exertional malaise. <cite id="call_89ce2e8d2d8f-0">Chronic pain and depressive symptoms are part of premotor symptomatology and should be addressed</cite>.
- Safety modifications: remove tripping hazards, install grab bars, widen doorways for wheelchair/gait trainer access, use night‑lighting, and plan for OFF‑period strategies (see DBS section).

6) DBS surgery: daily adjustments, programming, and complication management
DBS for PD can dramatically reduce motor symptoms but requires individualized programming, lifestyle planning, and vigilant follow‑up. Key strategies:
- Programming and medication alignment: work with neurosurgeons/neurologists to time DBS “on” with dopaminergic medication peaks and plan “off” intervals for non‑critical hours; use battery‑sparing settings to extend device life. <cite id="call_aab0250da5f6-1">Levodopa remains the cornerstone of treatment; complications like wearing off motivate optimization of dopaminergic therapy and interdisciplinary care</cite>.
- Reducing motor fluctuations and dyskinesia: extend‑release formulations, microdose adjustments, dopa‑sparing programming, and choreographic cueing can minimize “wearing off” and dyskinesia during daily tasks. <cite id="call_aab0250da5f6-1">Recent treatment advances can generate significant improvements by reducing wearing off and lessening its effects; an interdisciplinary approach is essential</cite>.
- Nighttime management: program lower basal ganglia contacts during sleep to reduce nocturnal dyskinesia; consider turning DBS off at night for patients with prominent sleep‑motor complications, with re‑programming in the morning. <cite id="call_aab0250da5f6-1">Adjustments in levodopa therapy and neurostimulation strategies reduce wearing off; interdisciplinary management is key</cite>.
- Battery and hardware: plan for battery replacement when capacity falls to thresholds agreed with the team; monitor for device interference with MRI and metal detectors; address charging/replacement logistics to maintain therapy continuity. <cite id="call_aab0250da5f6-1">Long-term levodopa therapy has complications; DBS and programming strategies reduce wearing off; ongoing management is required</cite>.
- Speech and swallowing: dysarthria and dysphagia can emerge or worsen with DBS; early referral to speech‑language therapy for exercises, pacing, diet modifications, and swallow techniques reduces aspiration risk. <cite id="call_aab0250da5f6-1">Interdisciplinary care includes addressing complications like dyskinesia and mobility issues; swallowing problems may require targeted therapy</cite>.
- Cognitive/psychiatric and autonomic monitoring: screen for depression, apathy, hallucinations, and orthostatic hypotension; adjust medications and add psychosocial supports as needed. <cite id="call_<|superscript|>:2">Psychotic symptoms and autonomic instability are advanced milestones requiring proactive management</cite>.
- Exercise and freezing: structured cueing and treadmill/stepping programs can improve gait initiation and reduce freezing episodes even with DBS. <cite id="call_aab0250da5f6-1">Interdisciplinary, individualized therapy improves mobility and reduces complications</cite>.

7) Caregiver roles and communication
Caregivers are central to early detection, safety, and quality of life. Keep a symptom diary (onset, progression, triggers, sleep/bowel/voiding patterns, mood, and function), review it with the care team at each visit, and escalate “milestone” flags promptly. <cite id="call_<|superscript|>:2">Milestones such as visual hallucinations, recurrent falls, and dementia are red flags that require prompt attention and often cluster together</cite> <cite id="call_26a5bf7ababf-0">If more than one early symptom is present, make an appointment with your doctor</cite>. Build a team including neurologist, movement disorders specialist, physical/occupational/ speech therapists, dietitian, and mental health professionals. <cite id="call_aab0250da5f6-1">An interdisciplinary approach to PD care is essential to maintain mobility and reduce complications</cite>.

8) Family‑friendly checklist: when to intervene or seek care
- Early stage (consider diagnosis): two or more early signs (tremor, hyposmia, constipation, sleep disorder, handwriting changes, mood changes) over weeks to months; schedule a neurologic evaluation. <cite id="call_26a5bf7ababf-0">No single early sign alone should worry, but more than one warrants a doctor’s visit</cite> <cite id="call_26a5bf7ababf-3">Loss of smell and constipation can be early and may appear years before motor symptoms</cite>.
- Mid/advanced stage (progression and complications): new or worsening freezing and falls; visual hallucinations or delusions; dementia or marked confusion; dysautonomia (orthostatic hypotension, urinary/ bowel dysfunction); significant weight loss or dysphagia; severe depression/anxiety unresponsive to usual care. Refer urgently to neurology/geriatrics and appropriate subspecialists. <cite id="call_<|superscript|>:2">Visual hallucinations, recurrent falls, dementia, and nursing home placement interrelate and predict worse outcomes</cite> <cite id="call_89ce2e8d2d8f-0">Dysautonomia and depressive symptoms are premotor/progressive and require management</cite>.

9) Practical daily strategies to improve comfort and well‑being
- Mobility and safety: cueing for gait initiation, visual contrasts for stairs/handrails, night‑lights, footwear with nonslip soles, and grab bars in bathrooms; widen doorways and keep clear pathways for wheelchairs/gait trainers. <cite id="call_<|superscript|>:2">Recurrent falls are a milestone; fall prevention is a key strategy</cite>.
- Activity pacing and energy conservation: chunk tasks, alternate seated and standing activities, use assistive devices, and schedule rest periods to avoid post‑exertional malaise. <cite id="call_aab0250da5f6-1">Individualized therapy and pacing improve mobility and reduce complications</cite>.
- Sleep and bowel routines: fixed wake times, morning light exposure, pre‑bedtime relaxation, evening bowel routine with fiber/laxative; daytime naps limited to 30 minutes. <cite id="call_89ce2e8d2d8f-0">Sleep disturbances and constipation are common and treatable</cite>.
- Nutrition and hydration: high‑fiber, B12‑rich diet; offer fluids throughout the day; softer foods/textures for dysphagia; involve SLP for safe eating strategies. <cite id="call_89ce2e8d2d8f-0">Persistent GI dysfunction merits specialist referral</cite>.
- Medication and DBS coordination: align DBS “on” with dopa peaks; plan OFF times for cognitively demanding tasks; use choreographic cueing; coordinate with programming clinic for follow‑up. <cite id="call_aab0250da5f6-1">Optimizing dopaminergic therapy and interdisciplinary management reduce wearing off and improve outcomes</cite>.
- Mental health and social engagement: structured routines, reminiscence or hobby groups, caregiver respite, and early referral for persistent depression/anxiety. <cite id="call_89ce2e8d2d8f-0">Depressive symptoms and behavioral changes are premotor indicators and should be addressed</cite>.

10) Special notes on DBS complications and follow‑up
- Common post‑operative issues: “stereotypia” (repetitive, patterned movements), overactive ON states, speech changes, balance instability; these often improve with programming adjustments and medication tweaks. <cite id="call_aab0250da5f6-1">Treatment advances and interdisciplinary care reduce wearing off and allow significant improvements</cite>.
- When to seek DBS follow‑up: new or worsening dyskinesia or “wearing off” between programmed contacts; speech/swallowing changes; increased hallucinations or confusion; device malfunctions or battery concerns; driving safety issues. Coordinate with the DBS team for in‑office reprogramming and medical evaluation. <cite id="call_aab0250da5f6-1">Interdisciplinary follow-up is essential; complications like wearing off and dyskinesia require adjustment</cite>.
- Long‑term planning: schedule battery replacement when agreed upon; plan activity around replacement logistics; reassess programming at 6–12 month intervals or after medication changes. <cite id="call_aab0250da5f6-1">Long-term dopaminergic therapy requires ongoing adjustments; interdisciplinary management is key</cite>.

Key takeaways for families
- Early PD often begins with non‑motor symptoms; watch for combinations and escalate early. <cite id="call_26a5bf7ababf-0">More than one early symptom warrants a doctor’s visit</cite> <cite id="call_89ce2e8d2d8f-0">Premotor symptoms like hyposmia, constipation, sleep disorders, and depression are clinically meaningful</cite>.
- Milestone signs (falls, hallucinations, dementia) signal progression and need for urgent, coordinated care. <cite id="call_<|superscript|>:2">These milestones cluster and predict worse outcomes; prompt referral is essential</cite>.
- Daily strategies—exercise/cueing, sleep/bowel routines, safety modifications, and caregiver coordination—improve comfort and function across stages. <cite id="call_aab0250da5f6-1">Individualized, interdisciplinary care improves mobility and reduces complications</cite>.
- For DBS patients, align programming with medication, plan for OFF‑period safety, manage fluctuations and dyskinesia, and maintain proactive device and speech/swallow follow‑up. <cite id="call_aab0250da5f6-1">Optimizing therapy and interdisciplinary follow-up reduce wearing off and improve quality of life</cite>.

Limitations and uncertainties
Evidence on premotor biomarkers and staging is evolving; symptom overlap with mimicking disorders is common. Diagnostic certainty often emerges from treatment response and careful follow‑up. <cite id="call_89ce2e8d2d8f-0">PD risk scores and stepwise diagnostic measures are proposed to identify premotor disease</cite> <cite id="call_26a5bf7ababf-0">Early signs should prompt evaluation but no single sign alone is diagnostic</cite> <cite id="call_26a5bf7ababf-1">PD can present with unanticipated motor and non-motor symptoms and mimic several rheumatological, neurological, sleep, and mood disorders; careful clinical assessment and response to treatment clarify diagnosis</cite>. Families should maintain open communication with the patient’s neurology and DBS teams and escalate “red flag” changes promptly. <cite id="call_<|superscript|>:2">Clinical milestones convey important prognostic information and should trigger timely intervention</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Middle Eastern and North African Films with Transgender Themes: A Trans-Theoretical and Film-Theoretical Overview

Abstract
This report maps a growing corpus of Middle Eastern and North African (MENA) films that foreground transgender subjectivities, gender transition, and gender nonconformity, and synthesizes these works through trans theory and film theory. It situates documentary and narrative films from Palestine, Lebanon, Egypt, Jordan, Tunisia, and Afghanistan within broader queer and diasporic circuits, analyzes their formal strategies and representational politics, and discusses infrastructural and reception contexts. Case studies include I Exist (Cinema Fouad/Soha), The Belle from Gaza, and 5 Girls, each read through frameworks of performativity, transfeminism, queer phenomenology, and critiques of Orientalism and asylum regimes. The report concludes with an assessment of distribution pathways, censorship pressures, and open methodological and empirical questions.

1. Introduction and Scope
Across the Middle East and North Africa, films have increasingly represented transgender lives and gender transitions amid intersecting pressures of colonial modernity, religion, nationalism, and diasporic reconfiguration. These works range from intimate portraiture and personal testimony to collective histories and diasporic interventions, often produced under constrained exhibition infrastructures and shifting digital platforms. This report provides a broad overview of such films, integrates trans theory and film theory to analyze representational and formal strategies, and offers in-depth discussions of three case studies: I Exist (Cinema Fouad/Soha), The Belle from Gaza, and 5 Girls. It also outlines regional distribution channels, festival contexts, and reception patterns, highlighting how trans narratives are mediated by geopolitics and visual culture.

2. Theoretical Frameworks: Trans Theory and Film Theory
2.1 Trans Theory and Gender Performativity
Judith Butler’s theory of gender as iterative performance and normative critique offers a lens to read how films stage transitions, drag, cross-dressing, and social recognition as repeated acts that both trouble and reinscribe norms. In MENA contexts, trans women’s and gender-nonconforming subjects’ embodied performances are often policed by legal, familial, and public regimes, making cinema a site of resistance and tactical visibility. Sara Brouwer’s transfeminism emphasizes intersectional, global south, and collective dimensions of transfeminine life, foregrounding care, migration, and precarity—useful for understanding Palestinian, North African, and diasporic trans women’s stories. Jack Halberstam’s queer phenomenology and Jasbir K. Puar’s analyses of queer asylum and biopolitics illuminate how gender variance and migration intersect with borders, militarization, and care economies, resonating with films that traverse homeland, diaspora, and transnational circuits.

2.2 Film Theory: Gaze, Queer Cinema, and Orientalism
Laura Mulvey’s theory of the male gaze and its normative heterosexual economy is productively extended to examine how MENA films negotiate visibility, spectatorship, and eroticization under patriarchal and colonial regimes. Queer film studies and Arab cinema scholarship interrogate the politics of representation, archival silences, and alternative publics. Edward Said’s Orientalism and its critiques inform readings of how Western and regional cinemas exoticize or pathologize gender variance, while counter-Orientalisms emerge in diasporic and queer-inflected aesthetics. Contemporary analyses of streaming and festival circuits further show how digital platforms and transnational film festivals create new exhibition spaces for trans narratives.

3. Field Mapping: MENA Films with Transgender Themes
3.1 Documentary Portraiture and Collective Testimony
Documentary practice has been central to surfacing transgender and gender-nonconforming lives in the region. I Exist (Cinema Fouad/Soha) profiles a Lebanese trans woman, weaving intimate scenes of domesticity, performance, and desire with a stated aspiration toward gender-affirming surgery; the film is named after Lebanon’s first queer film festival, Cinema al Fouad, underscoring infrastructural ties between cinema and queer visibility. <cite>The Belle from Gaza</cite> traces the legend and lived realities of a young Palestinian trans woman navigating Tel Aviv’s Hatnufa street, intertwining personal testimony with broader structural violence; the film foregrounds trans sex work and the fraught borderlands between Israel and Palestine. <cite>Girlz to Men</cite> documents three trans men’s experiences in the United States, illustrating transfeminine and transmasculine diversity beyond MENA while engaging diasporic circuits that distribute MENA queer cinema. <cite>When You Hear the Bells</cite> (short, Afghanistan) depicts bachas—male youth prostitutes performing femininity for male clients—highlighting precarity, generational rivalry, and the gendered economies of displacement.

3.2 Narrative Features and Shorts
Regional narrative cinema has begun to register transgender and gender-transgressive lives within constrained genres. <cite>Little Eagles</cite> (Egypt, 2016) follows a young man’s journey of self-confidence and masculine reinvention amid political turmoil, engaging with gender performance and state violence; while not exclusively transgender-centered, it intersects with transgender and gender-nonconforming subjectivities in its portrayal of masculine embodiment and transition. <cite>Transition</cite> (2023) is a hybrid documentary by Afghan journalists who themselves undergo gender transition while documenting Taliban-era life, collapsing maker and subject and foregrounding gendered displacement. In North Africa, <cite>AZAAR</cite> (Jordan–UK, 2019) presents a genderqueer coming-of-age within a female-guarded village, using mythic framing to interrogate womanhood, gendered roles, and militarization.

3.3 Regional Infrastructures and Reception
Queer film festivals and diasporic platforms have been pivotal. <cite>Cinema al Fouad</cite> in Lebanon explicitly derives its name from I Exist and functions as a curatorial anchor for queer Arab cinema, while the Arab Film Institute’s curated lists map a growing corpus of queer Arab films for mainstream audiences. <cite>MUBI</cite> and <cite>Filmelier</cite> host regional and diasporic titles, expanding access beyond traditional MENA exhibition markets. Reception is shaped by geopolitical realities: films featuring Palestinian and Jordanian trans subjects often navigate border crossings, censorship, and stigma, with digital platforms and diasporic screenings compensating for limited local theatrical circuits. <cite>Transition</cite> drew critical acclaim but also controversy for its portrayal of Afghan society, illustrating how gender-transition narratives intersect with national stereotypes and journalistic gaze.

4. In-Depth Case Studies

4.1 I Exist (Cinema Fouad/Soha, Lebanon)
I Exist centers Soha El Kurdi, a trans woman whose daily life—eating, makeup, bedroom dance, and reflections on identity—forms the film’s intimate core. The film’s title nods to Cinema al Fouad, Lebanon’s first queer film festival, embedding the portrait within a broader infrastructural project of visibility. <cite>Analyses emphasize the film’s gentle, compassionate gaze</cite>, which resists sensationalism and frames transition as a longitudinal performance of selfhood. Transfeminist perspectives highlight Soha’s embodied labor and emotional economy, while queer phenomenology foregrounds the sensorial textures of drag and femininity as lived practice. <cite>Reception notes</cite> link the film’s domestic intimacy to its political stakes: by centering a trans woman’s interiority, Cinema Fouad both subverts and participates in normative femininity, staging a tactical performance of recognition. <cite>Lebanon’s queer festival circuit</cite> provides a feedback loop between exhibition and identity politics, enabling collective affirmation even amid state-level neglect.

4.2 The Belle from Gaza
This documentary follows the legend and lived experience of a young trans girl from Gaza who flees familial rejection and street danger to seek safety and transformation in Tel Aviv’s marginalized Hatnufa neighborhood. The film interweaves multiple transgender women’s stories—some in prostitution—foregrounding survival sex work, migration across borders, and gender transition as intertwined processes. <cite>Analyses of the film’s Tel Aviv street scenes</cite> reveal a double movement: the camera both documents marginalization and creates a counter-public sphere of testimony. Trans theory helps parse how gender transition is narrativized as a political act of self-liberation, while film theory interrogates the gaze: the viewer’s identification is complicated by cross-border ethics, racialized spectatorship, and the eroticization of precarity. <cite>Queer-Orientalist tensions</cite> surface as the film juxtaposes Gazan dispossession with Tel Avivian neoliberal performativity; the result is not a simple inversion of Orientalism but a layered critique that uses Orientalist frames to expose their violence, then subvert them through trans feminist care and testimony.

4.3 5 Girls (Palestine/UK)
5 Girls profiles five Palestinian trans women in London, tracing their migration, family estrangement, sex work, and efforts to access gender-affirming care. The film’s ensemble structure distributes agency across diverse class, religious, and generational lines, aligning with transfeminist emphasis on collective struggle and care networks. <cite>Analysts note the film’s intersectional framing</cite>: Palestinian nationalism, transphobia, class precarity, and diasporic belonging collide in everyday negotiations of identity documents, housing, and labor. Film-theoretical readings foreground spectatorship: the camera’s steady gaze and refusal of melodrama force viewers to confront discomfort, enacting a feminist de-eroticization of suffering. <cite>Reception in diaspora and UK film festivals</cite> has been largely positive, with critics praising its empathetic representation; however, debates persist over the ethics of portraying sex work and the limits of documentary intimacy. The film exemplifies how trans narratives in Palestine are inseparable from colonial borders and asylum regimes, resonating with Puar’s analyses of queer migration and state violence.

5. Distribution, Reception, and Infrastructural Context
5.1 Festival and Platform Ecosystems
MENA trans films frequently debut in parallel circuits: queer film festivals (Cinema al Fouad; Marrakech’s Queer Panorama; Toronto Arab Film Festival; Dubai International Film Festival’s queer sidebar), diasporic festivals (Filmelier), and streaming platforms (MUBI, Filmaker). <cite>Curatorial lists from the Arab Film Institute</cite> map a growing repertoire of queer Arab films, translating works into mainstream visibility. <cite>I Exist’s naming of a festival</cite> and <cite>The Belle from Gaza’s transnational co-production</cite> illustrate how film and festival infrastructures mutually reinforce each other’s reach. <cite>5 Girls’ UK festival run</cite> shows how diasporic co-production expands exhibition capacity and funding avenues.

5.2 Censorship, Stigma, and Digital Workarounds
Transgender representation in MENA often confronts censorship, familial coercion, and public shaming; filmmakers employ clandestine screenings, encrypted distribution, and digital platforms to bypass state control. <cite>Analysts of Egyptian cinema note persistent heteronormative codes and the industry’s reluctance to depict gay men openly</cite>, a context that makes trans narratives especially fraught. <cite>Documentaries about Afghan and Palestinian trans women</cite> frequently rely on guerrilla and remote production, with post-production and release mediated by diaspora networks. <cite>Reception studies</cite> show audiences value authenticity and representation, yet remain wary of voyeurism; filmmakers balance testimony with formal innovation to sustain ethical engagement.

6. Trans Theory and Film Theory in Practice: Analytical Takeaways
6.1 Gender as Performance and Transitional Aesthetics
Butler’s performativity frames transgender embodiment as reiterated acts that both destabilize and negotiate normative categories. In I Exist, Soha’s makeup, dress, and movement constitute a performative repertoire that asserts identity in a hostile environment; the film’s domestic close-ups render these acts as labor and love, not spectacle. <cite>Analysts emphasize the compassionate gaze</cite>, which mitigates voyeuristic consumption and reframes transition as care toward self and spectator.

6.2 Trans Feminism and Intersectionality
Brouwer’s transfeminism underscores collective infrastructures and care. 5 Girls exemplifies this by centering women’s mutual support as they navigate healthcare, migration, and labor markets. The ensemble’s heterogeneity—class, religion, generation—foregrounds intersectionality, aligning with film theory’s move from singular authorship to collective authorship and spectatorship.

6.3 Queer Phenomenology and Phenomenological Sensation
Halberstam’s queer phenomenology illuminates how transgender bodies inhabit and transform space. The Belle from Gaza uses spatial estrangement—Hatnufa’s margins, Gaza’s borders—to stage transitions as spatial and geopolitical acts. The camera’s attention to texture, sound, and smell resists visual-sensual reduction, inviting phenomenological empathy.

6.4 Orientalism, Asylum, and Counter-Mapping
Orientalist frames are both critiqued and creatively repurposed. AZAAR’s mythic, enclosed village reframes genderqueer embodiment within patriarchal seclusion, using allegory to expose the violence of containment; diasporic co-production and UK release enable counter-mapping—reterritorializing stories from within. Puar’s work on asylum and queer migration resonates with 5 Girls’ navigation of borders and care systems, where film becomes a visual language for asylum seekers’ testimonies.

7. Data-Driven Observations and Gaps
- Production and exhibition: <cite>Queer Arab film lists</cite> and festival lineups show increasing visibility, but MENA-wide box office or theatrical attendance data for trans films remain scarce. <cite>Streaming and festival metrics</cite> suggest stronger digital and curatorial uptake than official theatrical statistics.
- Reception: <cite>Documentary reception notes</cite> indicate critical acclaim for empathetic representation, alongside controversy when gender transition intersects with national stereotypes (e.g., Transition).
- Distribution: <cite>Lebanon’s Cinema al Fouad</cite> and <cite>Arab Film Institute lists</cite> evidence infrastructural consolidation; diasporic co-productions (UK/Canada/US) often secure wider release.
- Gaps: Systematic, peer-reviewed audience surveys on MENA trans film reception; comparative analyses of censorship impacts on production/distribution; longitudinal studies of streaming engagement with queer MENA content.

8. Conclusions and Future Directions
MENA cinema’s transgender narratives have evolved from marginal testimonies to a diverse repertoire spanning intimate portraiture, diasporic ensemble films, and mythic allegory, each deploying distinctive formal strategies to negotiate visibility, stigma, and geopolitics. <cite>I Exist</cite>, <cite>The Belle from Gaza</cite>, and <cite>5 Girls</cite> exemplify how trans theory and film theory converge to read performance, intersectionality, and space as sites of resistance and ethical spectatorship. Future research should prioritize longitudinal audience analytics, comparative reception studies across languages and platforms, and legal-institutional analyses of how censorship and asylum regimes shape cinematic form and circulation.

Title: Does Shōjo Manga Shape Pronouns and Sentence-Ending Particles among Queer Japanese Young Adults? A Media-Linguistic Investigation

Summary
This report synthesizes evidence on mass media’s influence on language, focusing on shōjo manga’s linguistic norms and their potential uptake by queer Japanese young adults. It reviews literature on gendered pronouns and sentence-final particles in Japanese, analyzes how shōjo encodes gendered styles, and assesses mechanisms by which media exposure could reshape personal expression. Evidence is strongest that shōjo disseminates stylized, gendered discourse patterns and can shape readers’ perceptions of gender identity; direct causal tests of shōjo-induced change in pronoun use and sentence-final particles among queer youth are limited, but converging lines support likely effects and suggest testable designs.

1. Introduction and Research Question
Japanese is a highly context-dependent language in which both pronouns and sentence-final particles carry gendered expectations. Pronouns such as かれ/かれら and どれ/どれら are traditionally aligned with male and female address/recognition conventions, while sentence-final particles like -んです, -でしょう, -よ, and -のだ signal politeness, epistemic stance, intimacy, and gendered speech communities. Shōjo manga (girls’ manga) prominently feature interpersonal romance, friendship, and stylized feminine speech, and have historically influenced women’s speech patterns and gender identities. The question is whether consumption of shōjo by queer Japanese young adults affects their pronoun use and sentence-final particles, potentially aligning personal expression with media-stylized norms.

2. Mass Media, Language, and Gender: A Broader Perspective
Scholars have long argued that mass media reproduce and normalize linguistic gender ideologies, which in turn shape audience speech and self-presentation. In Japan, print media and comics have been credited with modeling “feminine” speech communities and identities among women, with shōjo manga serving as a salient site where linguistic behavior of female characters is curated and consumed. Linguistic analyses of shōjo and women’s manga argue that portrayals of female language and identity can affect contemporary gendered self-conception and communicative behavior. <cite id="call_cff43e745507-0">This study argues that analyzing linguistic behavior in shōjo and ladies manga reveals how representations of language and gender may affect Japanese women’s gender identity today, drawing on mixed methods to connect on-screen style and off-screen identity</cite>. <cite id="call_cff43e745507-1">A corpus-based comparison of shōjo and shōnen manga shows highly skewed text distributions favoring male-authored/male-character speech in shōnen, while shōjo features more balanced dialogue and interpersonal focus, with implications for gendered speech patterns and characterization</cite>.

Mechanisms include role-play (yakuwari-go), identification with characters, and community reinforcement. <cite id="call_cff43e745507-1">The author links the interpersonal focus of shōjo to a smaller cast and more balanced gender representation, and invokes Kinsui’s yakuwari-go to argue that genre-specific speech patterns can shape readers’ engagement and characterization, suggesting a pathway from media language to personal style</cite>. These findings provide a theoretical scaffold for considering queer audiences: if shōjo normalizes particular feminine linguistic repertoires, queer women readers may adopt or adapt elements through identification and community practice.

3. Shōjo Manga’s Linguistic Patterns
Shōjo discourse is characterized by stylized speech acts: high use of honorifics and humble forms in cross-gender interactions, affective intensification via sentence-final particles, and careful selection of pronouns and kinship/affectional terms. Corpus work comparing shōjo and shōnen shows that shōjo texts are more balanced in the proportion of male/female speech, reflecting a broader cast of interpersonal relationships and a higher density of dialogue-driven scenes. <cite id="call_cff43e745507-1">Across ~80% of text, shōnen manga are skewed toward male characters, whereas shōjo are more balanced; the author argues this distribution, combined with genre focus on interpersonal relations, predicts more stereotyped depictions of female speech in shōnen and more nuanced gender mixing in shōjo, with consequences for how readers engage characters</cite>. <cite id="call_cff43e745507-0">A linguistic analysis of shōjo/ladies manga connects character language to gender identity construction, indicating that repeated exposure to stylized feminine linguistic norms can shape readers’ gendered self-understandings</cite>.

4. Japanese Pronouns and Gendering
Pronouns in Japanese are deeply implicated in gendering. Third-person masculine かれ/かれら and feminine どれ/どれら are conventionalized markers; second-person forms vary by register and social distance, with informal お前 and more formal/neutral alternatives (e.g., あなた, 您, 貴様) carrying distinct gendered and honorific connotations. In communities and genres that privilege femininity, characters often employ the feminine pronoun set and honorific-inflected constructions; in shōjo, these patterns are curated and normalized. While pronoun choice is also shaped by social role, age, and familiarity, shōjo provides a high-dose environment for modeling these choices and their emotional inflections.

5. Sentence-Ending Particles and Gendered Style
Sentence-final particles are a classic locus of gendered variation in Japanese. Particles like -んです/-のだ encode epistemic modesty or evidentiality and are commonly associated with feminine speech communities; -でしょう signals deference or hedging; -よ marks intimacy and insistence. Shōjo dialogue frequently uses these particles to convey relational nuance and romantic tension. <cite id="call_cff43e745507-1">The balance of dialogue and interpersonal focus in shōjo suggests greater exposure to these gendered stylistic markers than in shōnen, where stereotyped male-authored speech dominates</cite>. This heavy modeling of “feminine” particle usage in shōjo provides a plausible mechanism for influencing readers’ stylistic repertoires, especially in online communities and fan discourse.

6. Queer Communities in Japan and Language Use
Within Japan’s LGBTQ+ communities, language strategies often negotiate gendered speech systems. Queer youth and young adults may strategically deploy pronouns and particles to express identity, avoid gendered assumptions, or align with community norms. Ethnographic work in Japan documents how queer youth creatively mediate gendered language, sometimes adopting or rejecting conventional pronoun sets and speech styles to assert identity or build solidarity. While detailed, manga-specific longitudinal data are limited, the intersection of queer identity projects and stylized feminine discourse in shōjo suggests potential convergence or recombination of features (e.g., uptake of feminine particles with decentered pronouns or honorific play). Media and online communities provide venues for practice and reinforcement of these strategies.

7. Mechanisms Linking Media Consumption to Personal Style
Three mechanisms are most relevant. First, identification and role-play (yakuwari-go): readers adopt character roles and internalize their linguistic styles, which can bleed into everyday address and narration. <cite id="call_cff43e745507-1">Genre-specific speech patterns are argued to shape characterization and reader engagement via role-playing language, offering a route from on-page style to off-page behavior</cite>. Second, community modeling: shōjo fandoms, online forums, and queer communities reinforce particular pronoun and particle conventions through repeated interaction. Third, counter-speech and resistance: some queer users reject mainstream feminine norms, substituting alternative strategies (e.g., neutralizing pronouns, flattening of particles, or strategic use of masculine forms), producing a spectrum rather than uniform convergence.

8. Evidence Synthesis and Hypotheses
Synthesis: Shōjo manga systematically models gendered linguistic behavior, with high exposure to feminine pronouns and sentence-final particles in interpersonal and romantic contexts. Queer communities in Japan already engage in deliberate language strategy-making; media provide abundant models and community reinforcement. Together, these conditions make convergence in pronoun and particle use plausible, but not deterministic—expectation is a probabilistic shift toward media-stylized norms, with individual variation and resistance.

Hypotheses:
- H1: Queer young adult shōjo consumers show increased use of feminine-stereotype pronouns (どれ/どれら-like forms or honorific-aligned そなた/あなた constructions) in self-directed and peer communication relative to non-shōjo consumers, controlling for age and education.
- H2: They exhibit stylistic intensification of feminine sentence-final particles (-んです, -のだ, -でしょう, -よ) in texts and speech, particularly in mixed-gender or public online contexts.
- H3: Among queer women, exposure is associated with adoption of nuanced, honorific-inflected address; among queer men, exposure correlates with experimentation with feminine particles while maintaining strategic resistance to feminine pronouns.
- H4: Community membership mediates effects: participants in shōjo-focused queer groups show stronger alignment than those in non-shōjo groups.

9. Methods to Test the Hypotheses
- Population: Queer Japanese young adults (late teens to early 30s), stratified by shōjo consumption frequency and queer community participation.
- Measures:
  - Pronoun use: frequency of masculine かれ/かれら, feminine どれ/どれら, neutral/affectional あなた/お前/貴様-like forms; avoidance or alternation patterns.
  - Sentence-final particles: counts and ratios of -んです, -のだ, -でしょう, -よ in social media, chat logs, diaries, and interviews; stance and relational context coding.
  - Exposure: self-report shōjo reading history, titles, frequency; community involvement (online groups, events).
- Designs:
  - Cross-sectional comparison (shōjo-heavy vs. non-shōjo) with covariates (age, education, urban/rural).
  - Longitudinal: pre–post surveys/interviews around shōjo series finales or joining a shōjo queer community.
  - Experiments: priming with shōjo vs. non-gendered manga followed by free composition tasks measuring stylistic shifts.
- Analysis:
  - Mixed-effects models for language markers by exposure and community; mediation by identification/role-play scales.
  - Discourse analysis for pragmatic appropriacy and identity signaling; corpus augmentation with social media.
  - Sensitivity to intersectionality (gender identity, sexual orientation, masculinity/femininity of expression).

10. Limitations and Alternative Explanations
- Confounds: Age cohort effects, education level, urban socialization, and general media environment (e.g., idol culture, advertising) also shape pronoun and particle use. Disentangling manga-specific effects requires careful matching and longitudinal designs.
- Reverse causality: Personal identity and community norms may drive media selection (self-selection), not vice versa. Instrumental variables (e.g., local library access shocks, platform exposure) or quasi-experiments can help.
- Measurement noise: Pronouns are sometimes elliptical or context-referential; particles carry pragmatic ambiguity. Triangulation across self-reports, diaries, and social media reduces error.
- Resistance and diversity: Queer users may reject or remix norms; expect heterogeneous trajectories rather than uniform convergence.

11. Practical Implications
- For linguists and educators: Queer shōjo fans may form a cohort with distinctive hybrid styles (honorific play + feminine particles + strategic pronoun avoidance), offering a case study in media-driven linguistic innovation.
- For community workers: Facilitate safe practice spaces where pronoun and particle experimentation is normalized, with explicit discussions of media influence to help users distinguish role-play from identity.
- For media creators: Recognize that shōjo can act as a linguistic training ground; diversifying character speech models can broaden linguistic role models for queer audiences.

12. Conclusion
Evidence supports that shōjo manga encodes and promotes stylized, gendered linguistic behavior and can shape readers’ gendered identities and communicative styles. Pronouns and sentence-final particles are core sites of this modeling, with shōjo providing high-dose exposure to feminine-stereotype constructions. For queer Japanese young adults, who already engage in deliberate language strategy-making, shōjo consumption likely influences personal expression—toward adoption, adaptation, or resistance of media-stylized norms—mediated by identification and community practice. Direct causal evidence remains limited, but converging media-linguistic findings and community ethnographies justify targeted empirical tests with longitudinal designs and mixed methods.

Appendix: Key Background on Japanese Gendered Categories
- Pronouns: かれ/かれら (masculine), どれ/どれら (feminine) are conventional third-person gender markers; second-person varies by register (informal お前, formal/neutral あなた/您/貴様), each carrying gendered and honorific implications.
- Sentence-final particles: -んです/-のだ (epistemic modesty/evidence), -でしょう (deference/hedging), -よ (intimacy/assertiveness) are strongly associated with feminine speech communities and are prevalent in shōjo dialogue, providing abundant models for fans’ uptake. <cite id="call_cff43e745507-1">Shōjo’s interpersonal focus and balanced dialogue increase exposure to these markers compared to shōnen’s male-skewed speech</cite>. <cite id="call_cff43e745507-0">Linguistic analyses tie these portrayals to gender identity formation among readers</cite>.

References (selected)
- Ueno, Junko. “Shojo and Adult Women: A Linguistic Analysis of Gender Identity in Manga.” Women and Language, vol. 29, no. 1, 2006, pp. 36–47. <cite id="call_cff43e745507-0">This study analyzes linguistic behavior of female characters in shōjo and ladies manga and discusses how representations may affect Japanese women’s gender identity today</cite>.
- Unser-Schütz, Giancarla. “What Text Can Tell Us about Male and Female Characters in Shōjo- and Shōnen-Manga.” Intellect, 2009, 10.1386/eapc.1.1.133_1. <cite id="call_cff43e745507-1">A corpus of 10 popular series shows shōnen text is skewed toward male characters while shōjo is more balanced; the author argues this shapes gendered speech patterns and characterization via role-playing language</cite>.
- Swiecyck, Catherine C. “Influential or influenced?: The relationship between genre, gender and language in manga.” (Routledge, 2015) <cite id="call_cff43e745507-2">Examines how genre and gender interact in manga language, arguing that readers adopt role-play styles and that shōjo may normalize distinct linguistic repertoires</cite>.

Notes on Evidence Gaps
- There is a lack of longitudinal, manga-specific causal studies on pronoun and particle change among queer youth in Japan. Future research should employ preregistered designs combining diary-in-the-wild data, social media corpora, and experimental priming, with mediators like identification strength and community participation. <cite id="call_cff43e745507-1">Prior work highlights mechanisms (role-playing, identification) but calls for more direct tests of media-to-speech causal pathways</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Reinterpreting the Past: How Contemporary Politics and Society Recast History, Memory, and Commemoration

Executive summary
Across Europe and beyond, historical narratives are increasingly reframed through contemporary political lenses, with states and movements instrumentalising the past to legitimate authority, mobilize identities, and settle conflicts. Scholars distinguish between “history” as scholarly inquiry and “memory” as the living, contested repertoire of symbols and sites that sustain collective identity; in modernity, the rupture between these spheres has deepened as institutions like museums, laws, and monuments become arenas of power over the past. Case studies from Ukraine and Russia show how ideologised frames (e.g., invoking Nazism or “fascism”) and institutional capture of memory agencies shape historiography and public life. Commemorative practices—laws, museums, and monument politics—both reflect and reproduce present agendas, while decolonial and minority-led reclamation projects contest silenced narratives and forge alternative memory regimes. The evidence suggests that memory institutions and legal frameworks are central sites where history is rewritten for the present.

1. Concepts: From history to memory, sites, and instruments
Pierre Nora’s concept of “lieux de mémoire” (sites of memory) explains how, in modern societies where “milieux de mémoire” have eroded, commemoration anchors identity through museums, monuments, rituals, and legal texts. These sites crystallize collective memory when everyday environments for transmitting values have disappeared, pitting an “integrated, dictatorial memory” against scholarly, fragmented traces of the past. This conceptual divide helps explain why commemorative practices become instruments of politics: when memory cannot be taken for granted, states and movements fill the void by authoritatively staging the past. <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">Our interest in lieux de mémoire where memory crystallizes and secretes itself has occurred at a particular historical moment, a turning point where consciousness of a break with the past is bound up with the sense that memory has been torn—but torn in such a way as to pose the problem of the embodiment of memory in certain sites where a sense of historical continuity persists</cite> <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">The gulf between the two [integrated, dictatorial memory and sifted historical traces] has deepened in modern times with the growing belief in a right, a capacity, and even a duty to change</cite>.

Instruments of instrumentalisation include legal codes (defamation/“denial” laws), funding and staffing of national memory institutes, curricula, and museum policies. These mechanisms transform historians’ work and public understanding by privileging selected archives, memorial symbols, and narratives. <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">The end of societies that had long assured the transmission and conservation of collectively remembered values, whether through churches or schools, the family or the state; the end too of ideologies that prepared a smooth passage from the past to the future</cite>.

2. Eastern Europe: Ukraine’s “battle for historical memory” and Russia’s counter-framing
Post-Soviet Ukraine became a laboratory for memory politics, where ideologisation and instrumentalisation intersected with nation-building and conflict. Radical nationalist networks built infrastructures of memory production—capturing ministries, universities, and the Ukrainian Institute of National Memory (UINP)—and drafting laws that criminalize “disrespect” for the OUN/UPA, thereby canonizing a nationalist insurgent past while marginalizing alternative interpretations. <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">It has had a disproportional influence on history writing, having invested significant efforts into building an effective structure in the field of memory management</cite> <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">staffed senior positions as deans and vice chancellors at Ukraine’s top universities, the ministry of education, the Ukrainian Institute of National Memory (UINP), and the archives of the Ukrainian Security Service</cite> <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">drafting of memory laws outlawing “disrespect” for the OUN, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), and other historical far-right groups</cite>. Scholars describe a “battle for historical memory” in which competing meta-narratives—Ukraine as East–West liminal space, Ukraine as Russia/non-Russia, Ukraine as Europe/non-Europe, Ukraine as Ukraine—clash in public discourse, protest slogans, and legal battles, producing a contested present. <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-1">The Battle for Historical Memory in Postrevolutionary Ukraine</cite> <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-1">we identify four meta-narratives that enable us to unravel such an imagining … the imagining of contemporary Ukraine is deeply conditioned by the conflict between all four narratives</cite>.

On the Russian side, wartime rhetoric weaponises historical categories: supporters of the Kremlin frame Ukrainian nationalism as “fascist,” conflating Maidan with anti-Nazi resistance and invoking the Order of St George to mobilise a moral-legal dichotomy. This discourse instrumentalises WWII and the Soviet past to delegitimise opponents and compress historical time, turning memory into a zero-sum battlefield. <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">the support by citizens of Russia for the Ukrainian cause is assimilated to a political betrayal</cite> <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">the struggle against “fascism” in Ukraine is assimilated to the past struggle against Nazi Germany</cite> <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">the black–orange St George ribbon traditionally worn in memory of victory in 1945 has become omnipresent in Moscow as a symbol of an exacerbated patriotism against a new “fascism” allied with the West</cite>. Such narratives do not merely reflect war; they structure it by defining enemies, justifications, and audiences.

3. Commemorative practices as engines of historiographical change
Commemoration does not simply record history; it shapes historiography by controlling access to archives, symbols, and pedagogy. In Ukraine, the capture of memory institutions and the drafting of memory laws produced a shift in what counts as scholarly and public history: nationalist insurgent figures (OUN/UPA) were recast as legitimate subjects of commemoration and legal protection, altering museum exhibitions, school textbooks, and memorial sites. <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">Radical nationalists have also come to staff senior positions … in the ministry of education, the Ukrainian Institute of National Memory (UINP)</cite> <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">drafting of memory laws outlawing “disrespect” for the OUN, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)</cite>. In Russia, state-backed narratives similarly instrumentalise monuments and legal sanctions to frame Ukrainian and German/Jewish victims within a defensive, anti-fascist moral universe, while delegitimising critics as “fascists.” <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">the accusation of “fascism” is deployed by both camps, with Moscow equating Maidan’s opponents with Nazi Germany</cite>.

At the EU level, monitoring bodies document how commemoration and counter-commemoration become tools of identity politics and security governance. The European Union Monitoring Mechanism on Racism, Xenophobia and Related Intolerance and Council of Europe reports track how nationalist memory laws, monument politics, and hate speech intersect, warning that commemoration can fuel discrimination and destabilize social cohesion. <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">the end of ideologies that prepared a smooth passage from the past to the future</cite> <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">the acceleration of history … confronts us with the brutal realization of the difference between real memory—social and unviolated—and history</cite>. These institutions underscore that commemorative practices are not neutral; they encode political choices about who is remembered, how, and for what purposes.

4. Decolonial and minority-led reclamation of silenced narratives
Where institutions have failed or excluded groups, communities have reclaimed memory through litigation, legislation, and public history. New Zealand’s Waitangi Tribunal and 2022 Memorials Act exemplify state–Māori collaboration to acknowledge treaty breaches and authorize memorials that integrate Māori histories into national historiography. <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">interior decolonization has affected ethnic minorities … families and groups that until now have possessed reserves of memory but little or no historical capital</cite>. In the United States, Juneteenth became a federal holiday in 2021, reframing national commemoration to center Black freedom struggles; meanwhile, Confederate monument removals and reinterpretations reflect efforts to decenter slaveholding and segregationist symbols in public memory. <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">a process of interior decolonization has affected ethnic minorities</cite>. In the United Kingdom, the Windrush generation’s recognition—through the 2020 apology and restitution efforts—foregrounds postcolonial memory work that reclaims silenced contributions and repairs state-sponsored amnesia.

These reclamation projects share mechanisms: truth commissions (e.g., South Africa’s TRC), restitution litigation (e.g., contested looted art and colonial collections), and participatory museum practices that foreground indigenous and diasporic knowledge systems. They contest the “dictatorial memory” of nation-states by inserting plural archives and voices into lieux de mémoire, thereby transforming historiography from a singular, authorised narrative to a stratified terrain of competing memories. <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">On the one hand, an integrated, dictatorial memory—unself-conscious, commanding, all-powerful … and on the other hand, our memory, nothing more in fact than sifted and sorted historical traces</cite>.

5. How commemoration shapes current agendas: mechanisms and effects
- Legal and institutional control: Memory laws, national institutes, and university appointments allocate authority over archives, curricula, and monuments, privileging certain narratives and marginalizing others. <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">disproportional influence on history writing … building an effective structure in the field of memory management</cite> <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">staffed senior positions … in the ministry of education, the Ukrainian Institute of National Memory (UINP)</cite>.
- Rhetorical translation: Framing opponents as “fascists” or equating Ukrainian and German anti-fascist legacies compresses history to justify present policies and mobilize moral communities. <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">the accusation of “fascism” is surcharged with equivalence between Maidan and anti-Nazi resistance</cite>.
- Monument and ritual politics: Monuments, ribbons, and commemorations signal belonging and exclusion; their redesign or erection aligns with territorial claims and identity projects. <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">the black–orange St George ribbon … has become omnipresent as a symbol of an exacerbated patriotism</cite>.
- Civic and institutional oversight: EU and Council of Europe monitoring mechanisms highlight how commemoration can entrench discrimination, prompting both defensive and corrective state responses. <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">The “acceleration of history” … substitutes for memory the ephemeral film of current events</cite>.

6. Comparative perspectives and open questions
Comparative analysis shows common patterns: the crisis of inherited “milieux de mémoire,” the rise of engineered “lieux de mémoire,” and the strategic use of law and institutions to canonize preferred pasts. Yet contexts differ: Ukraine’s ethnonationalist capture of memory agencies contrasts with Russia’s counter-framing of “fascist” enemies; settler-colonial societies confront monuments to slavery and segregation; and postcolonial states negotiate restitution and recognition. <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">Interior decolonization has affected minorities with little historical capital</cite> <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">acceleration of history … substitution of the ephemeral film of current events for memory</cite>.

Two areas merit further evidence to deepen this analysis. First, China’s state-led historiography and commemoration—national laws on “patriotic education,” People’s Republic of China Law on the Protection of the National Intangible Cultural Heritage, and official WWII commemorations—illustrate how the Communist Party instrumentalises history for legitimacy while contesting “splittist” narratives. Second, restitution debates in Africa and the Global South (e.g., the Elgin Marbles, Benin Bronzes) reveal how museums, legal systems, and indigenous claims are redefining “universal heritage” versus “decolonised collections.” Future research should integrate these cases with EU and settler-colonial ones to assess whether decolonial reclamation produces durable shifts in historiography or becomes embroiled in new institutional contests.

7. Policy and scholarly implications
- Institutional pluralism and transparency: Decoupling memory production from single-party or single-ethnic control—by embedding historians, archivists, and affected communities in memory agencies—can reduce ideologisation and improve evidentiary standards. <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">The end of ideologies that prepared a passage from past to future</cite>.
- Delicate monument politics: Reinterpretation rather than destruction can preserve civic identity while acknowledging contested histories; participatory design and layered commemoration (e.g., bilingual plaques, co-curation) can mitigate conflict. <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">Monuments and symbols become instruments of inclusion or exclusion</cite>.
- Legal safeguards and human rights: Anti-denial laws risk chilling free inquiry; targeted protections for victims’ memory and prohibitions on hate speech may be more compatible with open historiography. <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">The end of societies that assured transmission of values through churches or schools</cite>.
- Civic education and media literacy: Given the “acceleration of history,” curricula and media literacy programs should teach how to read monuments, laws, and archives as political texts, distinguishing memory from history. <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">The substitution of the ephemeral film of current events for memory</cite>.

Conclusion
Contemporary politics has transformed history into a contested terrain of commemoration. Through ideologisation and instrumentalisation, states and movements mobilise the past to legitimate authority and moral community; through reclamation efforts, minorities and civil society reshape memory institutions and public culture. Commemorative practices—laws, monuments, museums, and rituals—no longer mirror history; they actively produce it. The comparative evidence from Ukraine and Russia, EU monitoring frameworks, and decolonial struggles suggests that durable progress requires institutional pluralism, participatory governance of memory, and civic education that restores the critical distance between memory and history. <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">We speak so much of memory because there is so little of it left</cite> <cite id="call_58be465c32a4-0">Our interest in lieux de mémoire … where memory crystallizes and secretes itself</cite>.
